message.content: We now prove NP membership. A certificate lists the chosen vertices and edges. We verify by summing all vertex and edge weights to k. This verification process clearly runs in polynomial time relative to the total input size. Now we demonstrate NP-hardness by reducing from the well-known and widely established SUBSET SUM decision problem here. Given a set of integers and a target value k, the question asks whether some subset sums exactly to k. We construct a graph with one vertex for each integer, where each vertex i is assigned weight equal to a_i and no edges. Since there are no edges at all, any subgraph is just a set of vertices, so the total weight equals the sum of chosen vertex weights. Therefore, the given SUBSET SUM instance has a solution if and only if our constructed graph contains a subgraph whose total weight is exactly equal to the target k. This reduction is clearly polynomial since we create exactly one vertex per integer and zero edges, so the total construction time is linear in the total number of integers given to us. Since SUBSET SUM is NP-complete and our reduction runs in polynomial time, the graph subgraph weight problem is NP-hard, and combined with our earlier NP membership proof, we now conclude that the problem is NP-complete.
